title: Modular Arithmetic
body:
Arithmetic where you only care about the remainder. Fix a modulus $n > 0$; then

$$a \equiv b \pmod n \iff n \mid (a - b)$$

read "$a$ is congruent to $b$ mod $n$". Equivalently, $a$ and $b$ leave the same remainder
when divided by $n$, which is the [[Division Algorithm]] doing the work: every integer is
congruent to exactly one of $0, 1, \dots, n-1$.

This is the structural layer on top of the `%` operator [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]
teaches. There the remainder is a value you compute; here it is a *name for a class of
integers*, and the whole point is that arithmetic respects those names.

## The congruence classes are the objects

Write $[a]$ for the set of all integers congruent to $a$. There are exactly $n$ of them, they
partition $\mathbb{Z}$, and they are what $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is made of:

$$\mathbb{Z}_n = \{[0], [1], \dots, [n-1]\}$$

```
n = 5
[0] = {..., -10, -5, 0, 5, 10, ...}
[1] = {..., -9, -4, 1, 6, 11, ...}
[2], [3], [4] likewise
every integer is in exactly one class
```

Congruence is an equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), and that is exactly
what licenses treating a class as a single object. Same move as [[Sets]] in [[DISCRETE MATH]]:
give the collection a name and work with the name.

## It survives + and ×

If $a \equiv b$ and $c \equiv d \pmod n$, then

$$a + c \equiv b + d, \qquad ac \equiv bd \pmod n$$

so you may reduce **at any point in a calculation** rather than at the end. That single fact is
the whole computational value of the subject:

```
7^100 mod 5, without computing 7^100
    7 ≡ 2 (mod 5)
    7^100 ≡ 2^100 (mod 5)
    2^4 = 16 ≡ 1 (mod 5)
    2^100 = (2^4)^25 ≡ 1^25 = 1 (mod 5)
```

**Modular exponentiation** is that trick made into an algorithm: square and reduce, square and
reduce, so the numbers never grow past $n^2$ no matter how large the exponent. That is why
public-key schemes are computable at all, and it belongs to [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]], which
is where RSA lives.

Division does **not** survive in general, and that is the interesting failure. $2 \cdot 3 \equiv
2 \cdot 0 \pmod 6$ but $3 \not\equiv 0$, so you cannot cancel the 2.

## $\mathbb{Z}_n$ as a structure

$\mathbb{Z}_n$ with $+$ and $\times$ is a [[Ring]], and under addition alone it is the
[[Cyclic Group]] of order $n$ generated by $[1]$. Which elements have multiplicative inverses is
settled by the [[Euclidean Algorithm]]:

$$[a] \text{ is invertible in } \mathbb{Z}_n \iff \gcd(a, n) = 1$$

because $\gcd(a,n)=1$ gives $ax + ny = 1$ by Bézout, and reducing mod $n$ leaves $ax \equiv 1$.
So $x$ is the inverse, and the extended algorithm is how you actually find it.

The consequence is the course's first real theorem-with-teeth:

**$\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a [[Field]] exactly when $n$ is prime.**

If $n = ab$ with $1 < a,b < n$ then $[a][b] = [0]$ with neither factor zero, a **zero divisor**,
and no field has one. If $n = p$ is a [[Prime Number]], every non-zero element is coprime to $p$
and therefore invertible.

## Linear congruences

$ax \equiv b \pmod n$ has a solution exactly when $\gcd(a,n) \mid b$, and then it has
$\gcd(a,n)$ solutions mod $n$. Solve it by running the extended [[Euclidean Algorithm]] to
invert $a$, or by dividing the whole congruence (modulus included) through by the gcd.

Systems of congruences with pairwise coprime moduli always have a unique solution mod the
product, which is the Chinese remainder theorem. It is the reason a computation mod a big $n$
can be split into independent small ones and reassembled.

## Where the vault already does this without saying so

- **[[Hashing]]** is $h(k) = k \bmod m$. The table slot *is* the congruence class,
  and the standard advice to pick $m$ prime is this note's theorem: a prime modulus makes the
  multiplicative structure non-degenerate, so patterned keys spread out instead of piling into
  a few classes.
- **[[Integer Representation]]** is arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$. Unsigned
  overflow is not an error condition, it is *reduction mod $2^{32}$* working exactly as
  specified, and two's complement is the statement that $-x$ and $2^n - x$ name the same class.
  See [[Complements]].
- **Wrapping an index**, `i % size`, is choosing the class representative in $0..size-1$. It is
  the same operation a circular [[Queue]] performs on its indices.
